newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightists, foes face off in Strasbourg.
newsitem.headline: French far-rightists, foes face off in Strasbourg.

text.p: Supporters and foes of France's National Front poured into Strasbourg on Friday for a congress called by Jean-Marie Le Pen to propel his far-right party into mainstream politics.

Tens of thousands of anti-Front demonstrators were taking specially chartered "freedom" trains and buses to the eastern city to protest against the three-day congress due to gather some 2,200 party delegates from Saturday.
Protesters saying they were mourning the death of democracy began shrouding the city in black.
A black flag was briefly hoisted on the spire of the towering Gothic cathedral, black flowers were planted outside the European Parliament and black bands wrapped around street signs.

Le Pen, a fiery orator who backs reinstating the death penalty and sending even legal immigrants back home, has vowed to launch an all-out assault on the political establishment in the campaign leading up to a March 1998 general election.
The two-round, first-past-the-post polling system has kept the Front out of parliament, and an Ipsos survey published on Friday said it would remain out if the election were held now.
But political analysts believe the Front could end up on the second ballot, potentially holding the balance of power, in 150 to 220 of France's 577 constituences.
The congress has deeply divided Strasbourg, whose Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann has called in 2,000 police to keep order during the dozens of demonstrations scheduled.

Kicking off protests from a city hall balcony, she told demonstrators that Le Pen supporters were racists. "While they are within our city walls, the whole city is rising up to reject fate and affirm its devotion to democracy," she said.

Le Pen opponents predicted that 50,000 or more protesters would take part in the main protest march on Saturday, including Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin, Communist Party head Robert Hue and Greens leader Dominique Voynet.

But Le Pen backers have concluded there is no such thing as bad publicity for their party, which is basking in the national spotlight in debate on illegal immigration, crime and joblessness which hit a record 12.8 percent in February.
"There are people who'd have you believe that the National Front congress is Nuremberg and Le Pen is Hitler. These people are ludicrous," Le Pen told RTL radio on Friday.
Some leaders of the governing centre-right have come out against the protests, saying they played into Le Pen's hands.
"These demonstrations are a major error," said Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary general of President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic.

The Front "knows it cannot win the election on its own. But it would score a great victory if the conservatives lost and the Socialist Party returned to power. So it will portray itself as the only hope of the Right against the Left," he said.
Le Pen, who won an overall 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election, chose Strasbourg for the congress because two years ago the Alsace region gave him his biggest score.
Though advised to ban the congress on grounds it threatened public order, mayor Trautmann let it go forward although she planned to lead Saturday's protest march.
Warning of possible violent clashes between Le Pen supporters and protesters, she has appealed for calm.

She also removed a statue of Joan of Arc, the mediaeval heroine who symbolises French national independence, from its pedestal near the imposing cathedral in Strasbourg's centre, to prevent Front backers from using it as a rallying point.
The Front responded by urging delegates to stay inside the Strasbourg conference centre.
